items.title: Voters face flurry of ballot measures that could transform elections across the country
items.author: SRS0=la73=IH=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content: In another setback for Trump’s efforts to inject more federal control into elections, a federal judge last week to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s found the U.S. Department of Justice’s efforts to collect voter rolls from states and use them to check for noncitizens illegally casting ballots is illegal. Most states refused to comply, often citing privacy laws, though some states agreed to give the Trump administration unredacted voter rolls.  Courts have so far dismissed 26 Justice Department lawsuits seeking to force  states to comply. The ruling constricts the Trump administration from using its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, program, a federal tool the administration was using to verify voter citizenship once it obtained the voter rolls. This week, Votebeat spoke to Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center, about the implications.

items.title: The Brewers had the means to end the Dodgers
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers.” - Pat Murphy, Brewers manager

They’ve gotten good at it.

Since 2018, when Christian Yelich arrived and kickstarted the current era of Brewers baseball into motion, they have the fourth-most wins in baseball. Since 2023, when top executive David Stearns stepped down and handed the reins to Matt Arnold, they’re second behind the Dodgers. Since 2024, when Craig Counsell left and Pat Murphy stepped into the manager’s role, they’re first.

In the meantime, they ran into failure, and they learned and got better and ran into failure again. They tried things that worked, hit limits — three times dressed in Dodger blue — and pushed and found more things that worked and pushed until they discovered exactly where they stopped working.

The whole process was not easy, was better and more productive for not being easy. You’ll see Brewers players talk about it, about Murphy’s standards and the expectations that can grate on them over the longest, most rigorous season in sports.

“You have to be a certain kind of player to play for Murph and to play here,” Yelich told reporters in August, after Murphy pulled rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt from a game for a lack of hustle. “You couldn’t coach that way throughout the league. You really couldn’t.”

You can see it in Murphy’s strategic needling of his own team, cutting violently away at anything that might dull their focus. And you can see it in his gentle praise, his doting in moments of doubt.

“All I know is that on Aug. 12, we have the best record in baseball,” Murphy said right after the Brewers got swept by the Padres, right before they went to Dodger Stadium and took a confidence-building three of four. “And if you've got the best record in baseball, you're still going to go through times like this when things aren't very good, and everything seems to go against you. But it's in your head that things are going against you.”

They practiced, got called out when they fell short, and practiced, and got praised when they hit their marks.

Last year, it led to 97 wins in the regular season, the most in baseball, but they got trounced four times in a row against the Dodgers. This year, the Brewers won 103 times in the regular season, the most in baseball, again. Faced with the Dodgers, again, they won four times in a row, and they’re going to the World Series.

“The end justifies the means. But what if there never is an end? All we have is means.” - Ursula K. Le Guin, 

If a genie or a god or a world-altering dream granted median baseball fans three wishes this spring, I think the most common ask would have been for their team to win the World Series, and the next most common would have been for the Dodgers  to win the World Series. A particularly enraged few might have asked for the Dodgers’ demise ahead of all else. And an even smaller, more conspiracy-brained sect would have sought the opposite: A third straight championship for the Dodgers, with the conviction it would create more conducive conditions for the introduction of a salary cap and a lasting shift in fortunes for their team.

Watching a physically compromised Shohei Ohtani lunge and flail through this postseason, watching him do everything but break down in the batter’s box, I was struck by the foolishness of those wishes, of the human impulse to overestimate our understanding of what we want.

The Dodgers being out is not the good part, not really. To seek a good outcome above all else is to disregard how you get there.

Baseball is too hard and too interesting to be squished into the tiny form of a pawn on a chessboard. It isn’t a game of design and construction so much as sculpture. The season sands teams down to an essence that can only be partly planned. It grinds away at players who absorb the losses, then struggle to shape what’s left into something productive.

The Brewers practiced and practiced. Through grit and grind and greatness, they sharpened themselves into a winning instrument that will be judged by the intrinsic value experienced on the field and on the screen, not for the money spent in creating it.

It must be said that the Dodgers did a version of the same, repeatedly molding and wielding the game’s heaviest blunt force object to generationally great effect. Last season, the Dodgers overwhelmed the Brewers, but needed every ounce of might to get past the Blue Jays. Only in that struggle did we achieve our fullest appreciation of what they could do, of their means. The end came at the last possible moment, and still far too soon.

When the Brewers came calling for this year’s rematch, the weakened Dodgers were the ones overwhelmed. The Brewers won this round decisively, but it didn’t feel like a grand conclusion. It felt like a simple demonstration of physics, like a wasted wish.

“There is no avoiding the fight, because stupid will blame the sheep for inciting the wolves.” - Spencer Hall, 

Major League Baseball, and the team owners whose interests it represents, has spent the year trying to convince the viewing public that baseball is like Rock, Paper, Scissors. The brute force of high payrolls and big markets will always crush the scissors of leaner operations, and no one in their billionaire’s club has the paper to overcome the rocks.

Scissors slicing up rock on the sport’s biggest stage won’t change a damn thing about what they want or what they do next. They’re going to chase the financial boon of self-imposed spending limits, possibly at the expense of playing the games, and they’re going to go on saying that the fans want them to do it. They were going to do and say that all along, whether anyone wanted it or not.

That they have successfully misled so many interested onlookers is the saddest, most infuriating part, and that it's so immaterial to their only interest (money) makes it worse. The sport earns its interest so relentlessly that they can self-sabotage to grow their margins.

There are baseball fans spending their precious emotional energy on rooting to watch less of Ohtani in his prime, on rooting for or against a flattened caricature, on trying to channel their interest through a convoluted string on a deranged cork board that never pointed to anything except more guaranteed riches for the richest people involved. Worse, there are fans convinced they didn’t want to watch at all who will be stunned — “stun” is the Brewers-inspired euphemistic verb of the moment for the Brewers, briefly supplanting “loom” as it relates to the lockout — that the best team in baseball just dispatched the Dodgers.

The pennant-winning Brewers are only stunning if you have missed the whole point, if you have been convinced to follow a boring, pointless shadow puppet routine staged 10 stories above the action. They are not a stand-in for small markets or a team-building philosophy or a piece in a billion-dollar game.

They are just a great team that practices what remains the oldest and best advice available in baseball: Keep your eye on the ball. ⚾️

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.title: New from Chicago: An urgent call to turn from broken economics
items.author: 555618737.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
Acclaimed economist James K. Galbraith sounds an urgent alarm: how conventional economic ideas and policies are unequipped to account for the most daunting challenges of our geopolitical moment.

Amid a mounting sense of American decline, Americans live with a new kind of dissonance: economists announcing that everything is fundamentally fine. Where growth is steady, unemployment is low, prices are (somewhat) stable, and stocks are high—what’s there to worry about? 

shows that this dissonance reflects a failure to evolve. James K. Galbraith’s incisive history of economic policy in this century is grounded in the fundamental problem that today’s experts are still deploying tools from all yesterday’s wars: obsolete economic ideas, measures, and doctrines focused on market functioning and crude economic indicators like output and prices. These methods, many of them honed a century ago against a vastly different social landscape, offer little hope in the face of today’s more existential threats. 

Such conventional policies, Galbraith argues, are increasingly ill-equipped to counter the daunting challenges of our moment—from inflation to trade sanctions, industrial cold wars, and climate change—and, left unacknowledged, are accelerating the end of the US economy as we know it. Shortcomings include the weak responses to the inflation of 2021–2022; the sanctions war against Russia; the rise of China; the weak and ineffective attempt at industrial revival; and the impending demographic crisis. All have roots in a flawed body of outdated economic thought that has been sustained for ideological rather than practical reasons. They now promise to hinder the United States in the emerging multipolar world. 

As Galbraith makes plain, for all the virtues of the market system, governments and their policies make markets possible. The ideas behind the policies—for better or worse—will determine the fate of the US economy—and new and better ideas are urgently needed. The alternative—sticking with economic ideas and policies we know and currently use—brings the power to destroy us all.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Question your questions
items.author: bounces+n4u44reogwfvhxdewq2t6h66329mwslhe4wp@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about when to ask questions and what sort of questions to ask. It can be almost automatic to ask questions in certain situation, but sometimes those questions cause more harm than good.

This week, I'm sharing a simple framework for when to ask questions and what kind of questions to ask when trying to keep your team on track.

Before you ask questions of your team, consider you’re asking those questions. You’ll often be asking for one of these two reasons:

questions are designed to gather information. “Why do we think this customer issue seems to be coming up a lot lately?”

questions are designed to elicit an answer from a predefined set of acceptable responses. “Which of these two features do we want to prioritize first?”

Be careful when you ask Discovery-type questions at the wrong time.

You’re in a tightly scheduled meeting with a specific end time, which is essentially . The meeting is wrapping up as people gather their things and push back their chairs, when the leader says, “Okay, we’re pretty much done here. Anyone have anything else they want to talk about?”

You can probably the collective groan from everyone else in that room.

Because the leader asked an open-ended Discovery-type question when they didn’t actually want to discover anything. Suddenly, anyone in the room has the power to keep everyone there indefinitely rather than getting the team out of there and back to work.

Instead, they could ask a Direction-type question like “Our next meeting is on Monday at 10:00 AM, right?” or just not ask any questions at all.

A tell that you should not ask a question is that you are either hoping no one will answer, or hoping for a very specific answer while dreading other answers. In this case, the leader is for silence or “Nope!” while dreading other answers like “Actually, this is slightly off topic but it’s something that I’ve been thinking about for a while…”

When you ask questions, there’s a very good chance will feel obligated to answer. Are you you want to hear that answer?

items.title: Ready for their close-up
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
Under a microscope, we observe reality in extremis and in mundanity. We observe it in that instant. The usual gets replaced by the current. The specific overwhelms the general. October baseball is nothing if not a microscope.

It presents us with no context, just the guts of the matter at hand. And we never get any better at wrapping our heads around the chaos in magnified form. Among 6-foot-4 lefty batters, is Nathaniel Lowe a stronger hitter than Shohei Ohtani? Observably, yes. Is Cade Smith made of reinforced steel and strikeouts? We can see no data points to the contrary.

Most of the time, it’s better to build your understanding of the world out of big, grounded truths even as anomalies zip in and out of the frame. The MLB postseason asks you to forget about the broad view for a month or so, but we aren’t very good at doing that. We try to hold both in our heads, and frequently get dizzy trying to pull it off. Is the Yankees’ roster construction inherently worse than that of the Rays, or was the roster as constructed just worse last week?

With the Brewers up 2-0 on the Dodgers in the NLCS and the Guardians victors over the Rays in Game 1 of the ALCS, here are some observations that are true at least for today.

Last year, the NLCS meeting between the Dodgers and the Brewers was a decisive drubbing in which Shohei Ohtani batted .357/.500/1.143 and tossed six scoreless innings for good measure. It was the magnum opus for an all-time player in an all-time season.

Conventional wisdom doesn’t change quickly. So it mostly holds that the Dodgers still have the brighter and higher-potential stars, despite Milwaukee again running up the best record in baseball. It’s true the Dodgers have the more famous lineup card, but the Brewers now boast the top talents. By regular season production, the Brewers have the two best players in this series — Jacob Misiorowski and Brice Turang — and by on-field pop in these playoffs, we’d have to add red-hot catcher William Contreras to the list ahead of any performer in Dodger blue.

Observation No. 2: The pitches are fast and frenetic

Of course, the condensed talent pool of the playoffs also means these aren’t just any fastballs.

More than 41% of all pitches thrown this postseason have been 94 mph or faster — with a few sizzling offspeed pitches even making the cut — and the increased exposure to velocity is not helping. Hitters are registering the worst October results off those fast pitches since 2013, when 94+ mph offerings comprised only 29.5% of their diet.

A full 17% of all pitches thrown have been fastballs up and out of the zone, with hitters managing only a .201  against them. While his dirt-scraping golf homer deservedly got the wows, perhaps revived Guardians avatar Jose Ramirez’s tomahawk blast off 99.9 mph heat at his eyes was the more impressive shot.

Observation No. 3: The pitch not challenged could make all the difference

Before Jake Bauers’ 12-pitch battle drained Yoshinobu Yamamoto in the disastrous third inning of Game 2, the Dodgers pitcher wanted to challenge a 3-2 call that gave Brice Turang a walk, but seemed to defer to catcher Will Smith’s inaction.

It’s not a sure thing that challenge would have been successful …

But the potential reward — a second out, which was followed by a Contreras flyout — would have changed the complexion of the game. Of note: The Brewers are also concluding each game with an average of 1.2 challenges remaining, compared to the Dodgers’ 1.0. An early challenge should spring from a confident position, but they are no less important than late challenges.

Observation No. 4: Relief aces are being worked hard

No one on the Milwaukee Brewers has thrown more postseason innings so far than Aaron Ashby, the lefty who, you’ll note, is not a starter. Six games into this playoff run, Ashby has appeared five times, with four of those appearances stretching more than an inning. In NLCS Game 2, he secured a five-out save, meaning he has now gotten one more out than starter Logan Henderson and three more outs than Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young.

Meanwhile, the Guardians have deployed lockdown closer Cade Smith in all six of their games, asking him for more than three outs on three occasions (though he tired in one of them, prompting manager Stephen Vogt to bring in Gavin Williams).

Though pitchers are often tasked with unfamiliar challenges in October, Ashby and Smith are relatively seasoned going multiple frames. Ashby did it 23 times in 2026, tossing the second-most innings in relief in MLB.

Smith recorded at least four outs to finish a game 11 times, sixth most in the majors this season (and really second among high-leverage relievers).

They probably can’t keep this pace up forever, but they are at least accustomed to the situation.

Observation No. 5: It’s Rays all the way down

The original architect of the Rays’ ways, Andrew Friedman, now runs the Dodgers. The next in line, Erik Neander, still runs the Rays. Another one-time Rays executive, Matt Arnold, runs the Brewers. And Kevin Cash, longtime manager of the Rays, came up as a coach with Cleveland under Terry Francona.

It’s hard to say if there is a consensus understanding of the Rays’ edge, the things other teams try to emulate. I would sum up The Rays Way, as practiced in various forms by the Friedman executive tree, as an ethos of maximizing the potential of the organization in every direction, a constant stance of fluidity and openness to experimentation.

Among the many things lost in the often-disingenuous discourse tornado around “analytics” is the fact that the secret sauce of the supposedly new school Rays edge is essentially optimized scouting and coaching. The tactics and transactions are evidence based — they’re not selling jeans — and probabilistic, but inside the system, it’s a human touch that keeps developing and unlocking the best version of players.

Each branch of the Rays tree has its own twists on this now. The Dodgers need no further explanation. Arnold’s Brewers have earned their own reputation for building the boat out of athletic, fundamentally sound position players and turbocharging them from there.

What’s increasingly clear is that efforts to distinguish small ball or Brewers baseball or the Rays way or old school or new school are sort of chasing shadows. With some caveats about how some free agent spending or salary bumps can and could be both beneficial and fan friendly, this is just how to run a good baseball organization now.

Every other club’s aspirations aren’t hidden in the details. They are plainly on display when Jacob Misiorowski winds and fires, when Brice Turang uncorks a swing, when Drew Rasmussen saws off yet another batter, when Josue De Paula waits in the wings for a call. Inspect and dissect as much as you like, but you’ll find the same signals in every deep-diving search. Someone who works or worked for the Rays will probably be building something new on top by spring. ⚾

An arbitrary Bandwagon fan ranking of the remaining teams

Every remaining team ranked by the team member for whom a World Series win would feel like a lifetime achievement championship:

  1. Guardians: Jose Ramirez is getting a statue in Cleveland regardless of whether he ever grasps the Commissioner’s Trophy. Even better if he whacks a key hit and gets to describe the pitch afterward.
  2. Brewers: Christian Yelich’s emergence as an MVP-level player invigorated the Brewers to start this era of dominance. As Sam Miller covered in his newsletter this week, he hasn’t had many postseason moments to add as a cherry on top, but he’s getting a chance to add those now.
  3. Dodgers: Tarik Skubal is the top candidate I suppose, but he’s not particularly close to the end, or particularly tied to the club just yet. I’m not even sure winning a ring with this Dodgers team would eclipse his put-the-team-on-my-back postseason excellence in Detroit.

MLB proposed a return to a 154-game schedule, a number last used leaguewide in 1960 (and in the NL in 1961). This would give players a standard weekly day off (Monday), theoretically creating some health benefits and potentially some attention-economy scheduling wins. It would certainly give your friendly neighborhood baseball newsletter writer a nice little window to breathe, reflect and write, but I’m nonetheless against the idea on the grounds of playoff creep.

The whole concept of fewer games, which I suspect actually does broadly appeal to players, is of course tied to the salary cap, like every other proposal MLB is throwing around for useless public relations points.

This is all a charade for now, but in the months when the fun is gone, you can see the start of what the sides might be discussing outside of the salary cap showdown.

It’s fair to seek some accountability for the Yankees being so mistake-prone so repeatedly on defense. There are good questions to be asked about how Cashman stuffs the roster with powerful but lumbering (or virtually immobile, in the special case of Giancarlo Stanton) hitters whose athletic limitations often tie his manager’s hands.

Then again, the Yankees’ track record of making the playoffs — even in what is often the league’s toughest division — and justifying high expectations is a very real high-wire act that could very much go awry with the wrong overreaction.

I expect not nearly as much will change in the Bronx as disappointed fans want right now, and the rearview mirror take on this post-2024 pennant era will be colored almost entirely by Cashman and the club’s success or failure in finding a next wave of position players to support Aaron Judge and roll ahead with Cam Schlittler.

Ben Rice looks like one building block, but he’s in the same offense-first (offense-only?) vein as every other recent titan. Is George Lombard Jr. a mainstay? Is Spencer Jones a real fixture? Is an external piece finally the missing, long-term piece that Jazz Chisholm, Trent Grisham, Paul Goldschmidt, et all just weren’t?

For now, the  plan is probably to wait and see. At some juncture, though, best will lose its grip and  will take the wheel.

After a massively disappointing season, Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. had eye surgery …

… which certainly raised my eyebrows.

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.author: SRS0=WFyy=IA=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content: I think we need to restore the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court has said that we can't do it by simply going back to the old 1965 list. But it does explicitly say that it's not hostile to a new pre-clearance formula, and there are any number of ways that we can devise them. But before we do that, we have to confront the very hard truth that, without a robust Voting Rights Act, we are seeing immediate, significant, and meaningful burdens on minority voters that result as a direct effect of the erosion of this law. So, what that coverage formula looks like should be up to Congress, but it's going to take actions by Congress in order to get this done. Whether the Supreme Court then looks at a new coverage formula and accepts it as a reasonable remedy, I can't say. But I think the evidence that we present in this book shows that it really should.
